```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

F and t tests rest on the model's distributional assumptions and, for mixed models, on
approximate degrees of freedom. With few experimental units, skewed residuals or a
GLMM, resampling tests are a useful check. predictmeans has:

- `permmodels()`: permutation tests of the terms and coefficients of `lm`, `glm`, `aov`,
  `gls`, `lme` and `lmer` models;
- `permlmer()` and `permanova.lmer()`: permutation likelihood-ratio tests for `lmer`
  models, including tests of random effects;
- `bootmodels()`: parametric bootstrap tests for `lmer` and `glmer` models.

The results of `permmodels()` and `bootmodels()` can be passed to `predictmeans()` and
`contrastmeans()` (argument `permlist`), which then give resampling p-values for pairwise
comparisons and contrasts.

The examples below use 99 or 199 resamples so that they run quickly; use 999 or more in
practice. The smallest p-value possible is 1/(number of resamples + 1). `ncore` sets the
number of cores used for the refits (`ncore = 1` here, as for CRAN checks); `seed` makes
the results reproducible.

```{r}
library(predictmeans)
Oats <- as.data.frame(nlme::Oats)
Oats$nitro <- factor(Oats$nitro)
fm <- lmer(yield ~ nitro * Variety + (1 | Block/Variety), data = Oats)
```

## Permutation tests of terms and coefficients

For linear models the response is permuted. For mixed models the residuals are first
decorrelated with the symmetric square root of their estimated covariance, permuted, and
correlated again (Lee and Braun 2012), so each permuted data set keeps the model's
correlation structure; the model is then refitted to each. (predictmeans 1.x used the
Cholesky factor, whose results depended on the order of the data.)

```{r}
perm <- permmodels(fm, nperm = 199, ncore = 1, seed = 1)
```

The tables repeat the model's tests with a `Perm_p_value` column: the proportion of
permuted statistics at least as large as the observed one.

For `lm` and `aov` models, `method = "freedman-lane"` tests each term by permuting the
residuals of the model without that term and adding them back to its fitted values
(Freedman and Lane 1983). Permuting the response rejects true null hypotheses too often
when a covariate with extreme values is related to the tested term (Anderson and
Legendre 1999); Freedman–Lane keeps the level there. It gives the tables only (no refits
for `permlist`), and it is fast:

```{r}
fm_cars <- lm(mpg ~ wt + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
permmodels(fm_cars, nperm = 999, type = "II", seed = 1, method = "freedman-lane")
```

## Pairwise comparisons and contrasts

The same refits give permutation p-values for pairwise comparisons, in the `pairs`
table and the legacy p-value matrix:

```{r}
pm <- predictmeans(fm, "nitro", permlist = perm, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE, ncore = 1)
pm$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "statistic", "p.value", "p.method")]
```

and for contrasts:

```{r}
cm <- contrast_family(Kmatrix(fm, "nitro"), "trt.vs.ctrl")
contrastmeans(fm, "nitro", ctrmatrix = cm, permlist = perm)[[1]]
```

`adj` adjusts the permutation p-values with any `p.adjust()` method or `"sidak"`.
`"tukey"`, `"scheffe"` and `"mvt"` need the t distribution and are not available with
`permlist`.

## Testing random effects: `permlmer()`

`permlmer()` compares two nested `lmer` models with a permutation likelihood-ratio test
(Lee and Braun 2012). This is useful for random effects, where the usual chi-square
reference distribution is wrong because the null value of a variance lies on the
boundary. Does the slope for `Days` vary between subjects?

```{r}
fm1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
fm0 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
permlmer(fm0, fm1, nperm = 99, ncore = 1, seed = 1)
```

`permanova.lmer()` applies the same test to each fixed term of an `lmer` model in turn
(Type I, II or III), for an ANOVA table with permutation p-values.

## Parametric bootstrap: `bootmodels()`

`bootmodels()` simulates new responses from the model fitted without its fixed effects
(an intercept and the same random effects: the global null hypothesis), refits the full
model to each and compares the statistics. Unlike permutation, it works for GLMMs.
For the clinical trial data (a binomial GLMM):

```{r}
data(Clinical)
fm_clin <- glmer(cbind(Favorable, Total - Favorable) ~ Treatment + (1 | Clinic),
                 family = binomial, data = Clinical)
boot <- bootmodels(fm_clin, nsim = 99, seed = 1)
```

Its result is used as a `permlist`; the `pairs` table then says `"bootstrap"`:

```{r}
pmb <- predictmeans(fm_clin, "Treatment", permlist = boot, plot = FALSE, prtnum = FALSE,
                    ncore = 1)
pmb$pairs[, c("level1", "level2", "estimate", "p.value", "p.method")]
```

## Which to use

- **Terms and pairwise comparisons in `lm`, `lme` and `lmer` models**: `permmodels()`.
- **Terms of `lm` and `aov` models with covariates**, especially skewed ones or ones with
  extreme values: `permmodels(method = "freedman-lane")`.
- **Mixed models with a covariate with extreme values**: the Kenward–Roger or
  Satterthwaite F test (`pm_joint()`, or `anova()` of an lmerTest fit); permutation
  rejected slightly too often there in a simulation study.
- **A variance component, or any comparison of two nested `lmer` models**:
  `permlmer()`.
- **GLMMs**: `bootmodels()`.
- With large samples and well-behaved residuals the F and t tests (with Kenward–Roger
  df for `lmer`) agree closely with these, at a fraction of the time.

## References

Anderson, M. J. and Legendre, P. (1999). An empirical comparison of permutation methods
for tests of partial regression coefficients in a linear model. *Journal of Statistical
Computation and Simulation* 62, 271–303.

Freedman, D. and Lane, D. (1983). A nonstochastic interpretation of reported
significance levels. *Journal of Business & Economic Statistics* 1, 292–298.

Lee, O. E. and Braun, T. M. (2012). Permutation tests for random effects in linear mixed
models. *Biometrics* 68, 486–493.
